reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes joining a BitClub-branded mining pool, paying at least 1% to obtain Bitcoin, and earning passive daily Bitcoin income through low-cost participation. Spoken encouragement to register, displayed pool figures, investment recovery estimates, and references to commissions place the claims in a recruitment and business-promotion context. The account page does not establish that payouts occurred or that earnings were verified, while the millionaire claim is presented as an unusually strong wealth claim rather than a guaranteed return.

opening.argument: The presentation includes meaningful caution rather than a risk-free promise. It explicitly says cryptocurrency trading is complicated and advises viewers not to attempt it without a year or two of study. The speaker also describes a long recovery horizon for mining investment, estimating eight months or more and personally expecting roughly ten or eleven months. Those qualifications are inconsistent with presenting effortless or guaranteed returns. The account example is further qualified as not being pure mining and as including commission, which signals that the displayed result is not a simple promise of mining profit.

citations.quote: this is very complicated and I do not recommend you to go there yourself, if, of course, you do not study there, for a year or two in this direction.
And we got that the average occupancy is from 8 months and above.
So I'll probably see my investment in about 10 or 11 months.
But this is not pure mining, of course, this is also a commission.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited price and income language should be read alongside these qualifications. A stated cost and an account demonstration establish that a service is being discussed, but they do not establish a guaranteed payout or deception. The reference side also treats the account page's figures as unverified while overlooking the speaker's express warning that the result includes commission and is not pure mining.

citations.quote: But this is not pure mining, of course, this is also a commission.
So I'll probably see my investment in about 10 or 11 months.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The warnings concern trading complexity and an estimated payback period; they do not withdraw the participation offer. The same presentation still says viewers should join the company and receive Bitcoin, and separately advertises passive daily income. Calling an account result partly commission does not verify that the advertised mining or commission system actually pays as represented.

opening.argument: The video's central structure is an educational presentation about cryptocurrency and blockchain. It announces that it will first explain cryptocurrency and blockchain, then discuss where money can be made, and proceeds through electronic money, decentralization, blockchain records, speculation, trading, and mining. The speaker also explains how a transaction becomes a hash and enters a block, while the slides visibly present blockchain concepts and mining pathways. A technology and operational demonstration can discuss a commercial example without becoming a deceptive solicitation.

citations.quote: at the beginning we will talk about cryptocurrency blockchain and the second part is be about how and where it can be made.
Blockchain is the open journal of all transactions.
These transactions get clouded up. There are certain machines that generate and account for this hash.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The educational framing does not erase what is actually demonstrated. The presentation moves from general explanation to a named company, participation instructions, pool purchases, and claimed earnings. Its own wording says the audience should become part of the company and get Bitcoin, so this is more than a neutral lesson about how blockchains work.

citations.quote: we have to be a part of this company and get our Bitcoins.
we have mined a pool for US$ 1.500

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The technical explanation and slides provide context, but the relevant commercial message is participation in a paid mining pool. The presentation does not merely explain hashing: it presents a company, pool packages, and earnings as reasons to participate. Educational material can still function as promotion when its practical conclusion is to join and obtain Bitcoin.

citations.quote: we have to be a part of this company and get our Bitcoins.
for starters we have mined a pool for US$ 1.500

opening.argument: The material can be understood as promotion of an ordinary mining service or business participation, with concrete operational limitations rather than a disguised guaranteed-return scheme. It discusses equipment, electricity, cooling, ventilation, maintenance, changing ASIC hardware, and an estimated recovery period. The speaker says participation involves a pool and fees, but the supplied material does not show a demand for credentials, a guaranteed return, or income from recruiting a downline. The existence of a paid service and referral contact is not by itself evidence of a scam.

rebuttal.rebuttal: This is not merely a generic service listing. The presentation asks viewers to join a named company, pay into a pool, and receive Bitcoin, while also presenting passive daily income and commissions. Equipment costs may explain the business story, but they do not establish that customer payments correspond to genuine mining capacity or that the advertised returns are reliable.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The existence of a pool fee and a business explanation does not prove that the pool is fraudulent. The cited language does not guarantee a return, and the presentation supplies operational discussion about mining expenses and hardware turnover. A referral link and partner support are compatible with ordinary commerce; they do not by themselves establish a deceptive mechanism.
